references.text: Abram built an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him—a parallel to the patriarchs' practice of worshiping God at key travel destinations.
Isaac went up to Beersheba; the Lord appeared to him that night, and he built an altar there—a direct parallel to Jacob's offering and God's revelation in Beersheba.
Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and called on the name of the Lord, the Eternal God, highlighting Beersheba's significance as a place of worship for the patriarchs.
Jacob refers to God as 'the God of my father Isaac' (pachad Yitschak), the same expression used in 46:1 where Jacob offers sacrifice to 'the God of his father Isaac.'
God instructs Jacob to go to Bethel and build an altar, illustrating Jacob's practice of offering sacrifices to God at major turning points in life.
God's promises to Jacob in Bethel to protect him and bring him back to the land—relevant background for Jacob's prayer and sacrifice before traveling to Egypt.
